cards.title: PDP hero image: lifestyle over white-background product shot
cards.summary: Treat the first PDP image as a split-testable asset and favor lifestyle/in-use imagery over sterile white-background shots.
cards.use_when: Designing or A/B testing the lead image and above-the-fold layout on a product detail page.
steps: Audit your PDP hero images: if the first thing a shopper sees is a bare product on a white background, flag it for testing.
Build a lifestyle alternative that shows the product in use, on a person, or in its real context, and test it as the PDP first image against the current shot.
Recognize that the image sits next to your description: a strong hero image plus weak copy wastes the real estate, so pair the image change with benefit-led headline copy.

Use Amazon-branded product pages as the reference standard for image density and optimization, since the source argues their traffic volume forces continuous testing of imagery and buy-button placement.
Treat this as an ongoing split test, not a one-time swap; first-image choice is called out as one of the more important PDP tests.
caveats: Source praises Amazon-style pages as the most optimized but does not provide a benchmark; your catalog may not support the same image volume.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Increase AOV on the PDP with frequently-bought-together blocks
cards.summary: Use bundled and multi-pack blocks on product pages to raise average order value, especially for multi-SKU catalogs.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a PDP or cart for a brand with multiple SKUs, packs, or add-on options.
steps: Identify the SKUs most commonly purchased together or that logically bundle (e.g., a product plus an accessory or different pack size).
Build a clearly laid-out 'frequently bought together' or bundle module on the PDP and in the cart, making the combined purchase easy to add in one action.
Design explicit pack ladders (e.g., six-pack vs 12-pack) so shoppers can self-select the larger option when intent is high.

Consider that the entry pack shapes repeat behavior: the source observed that a larger initial pack drives faster consumption and repeat purchase, so treat pack size as both an AOV and a retention lever.
Test placement and which bundle sits in the highest-visibility slot.
caveats: The source's claim that a 12-pack leads to faster repeat purchase is based on their own emerging data at year two; smaller stores may lack enough order history to confirm this pattern.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Strategic homepage offer placement by margin and inventory
cards.summary: Choose which offer occupies the homepage hero based on margin and the inventory you most need to move, not just what is newest.
cards.use_when: Deciding which product, bundle, or offer to feature in the homepage hero or primary merchandising slot.
steps: List your current offers and annotate each with its margin and any inventory you need to clear.
Place the highest-margin offer or the product you are trying to drive through inventory in the most prominent homepage position.
Define one clear 'big offer' for the homepage rather than diluting attention across many promos.
Continue down the homepage into category and insight layers so shoppers with many SKUs can browse and find feedback on a specific SKU.
Align the homepage hero choice with current ad traffic so the landing offer matches the ad's promise.
caveats: The source is expressing a preference for margin-driven placement; it is a judgment call, not a tested rule with published results.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Designing acquisition offers for a high-CPM environment
cards.summary: With CPMs running $35–$45 in the source's dataset, structure offers that give new customers something they cannot get elsewhere and set up later purchases.
cards.use_when: Building a new-customer acquisition offer when paid media costs are high and first-order economics are tight.
steps: Define the acquisition offer so it is clearly more valuable than simply landing on the website and is unique to buying direct.
Identify the single SKU or product that, when bought first, drives the most customer lifetime value, and make that the entry offer.
Plan the secondary and tertiary products that attach to that first purchase so the offer opens a path to repeat buys (e.g., a consumable plus a low-cost accessory).
Use the framework of two goals at any time: get existing buyers to spend more, or get more people to spend at all.
Within those two buckets, check margins to decide which offers you can actually afford to run.
caveats: The $35–$45 CPM range is the source's own dataset, not a universal benchmark; the source contrasts it with a pre-2020 era of roughly $10–$15 CPMs.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Use high-perceived-value, low-COGS gifts with purchase instead of discounts
cards.summary: Substitute or supplement discounts with gift-with-purchase items that feel valuable to the customer but cost the brand little.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to incentivize a first purchase or subscription while protecting margin.
steps: Pick a GWP item with high perceived value but low cost of goods (the source uses the example of a towel, scrunchie, cup, mug, or blender).
Run the arbitrage math: if the item's cost is $100 and it reduces CAC by more than $100, the GWP pays for itself, especially when back-end LTV is strong.
If the GWP mainly makes customers stickier rather than lowering CAC, you can still justify it by baking the cost into front-end acquisition and winning on the back end.
Use GWP-style offers to create different entry points into the brand beyond discounts, which the source argues are the primary lever for new customer acquisition as ad costs rise.
Consider giving a new product free to existing subscribers as a low-cost way to increase perceived value.
caveats: This is the source's stated framework for deciding, not a measured result; GWP effectiveness depends on your COGS and CAC, and may be less effective than a discount in some categories.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Organize offer testing by traffic source and margin
cards.summary: Structure offer creation as a system: first split by traffic channel, then by the two goals of more spend or more buyers, then check margin feasibility.
cards.use_when: Building a repeatable offer-testing calendar rather than improvising promos.
steps: Segment offers by traffic source (e.g., app, Google, Meta, Twitter, direct mail) because a customer from each channel carries a different expected value based on how long they stay and spend.
Collect the data needed to compare channel-level customer value before committing to channel-specific offers.
For each offer, ask whether the goal is to make existing customers spend more or to increase the number of people who spend.
Screen each idea against margin: can you afford this offer at all?
Set an operating cadence for how many unique offers go live per quarter; the source set a KPI of 15 unique offers in one quarter once the team was in place.
caveats: The 15-offers-per-quarter target is a source-specific KPI from their team capacity, not a recommended universal number.
Channel-level customer value requires enough data volume to be meaningful.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: A basic CRO and customer-data stack for a DTC store
cards.summary: Assemble a small stack for site speed, first-party data, heatmaps, custom page building, and customer identification.
cards.use_when: Choosing tools to support conversion optimization and first-party data collection on a Shopify-style store.
steps: Use a site-speed tool to monitor and improve load performance (the source cites Nostra, also used for first-party data).
Add a customer-identification layer to enrich email campaigns (the source was trialing customers.ai for user identification).
Install a heatmap and customer-experience tracking tool to see on-page behavior (the source cites heatmap.com).
Use a visual page builder to create custom landing and PDP pages without full dev cycles (the source was on Replo).
Verify current capabilities and pricing for each tool directly with the vendor, since interfaces and features change.
caveats: This is one brand's stack at a point in time; tool fit depends on platform, volume, and budget, and capabilities may have changed.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Design mobile-first and account for dark mode
cards.summary: Assume most traffic is mobile and design the full experience—including email—for mobile and dark-mode viewing first.
cards.use_when: Designing PDPs, landing pages, and email templates for a store whose traffic is majority mobile.
steps: Check your analytics for the mobile/desktop split; the source found roughly 75% of traffic was mobile after initially optimizing for desktop.
Design layouts, CTAs, and page structure mobile-first, then adapt upward to desktop.
Account for dark mode in email and on-site viewing: logos, text, and images should remain legible on dark backgrounds.
Test the ad and landing experience on mobile as the primary path rather than treating it as a secondary adaptation.
Optimize both experiences but let mobile drive the design decisions.
caveats: The ~75% mobile figure is the source's own traffic mix, not a general benchmark; verify your own split.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Judge email performance by revenue per recipient within segments
cards.summary: Track revenue per recipient (RPR) by cohort and segment rather than only at the list level, to see which audiences are worth sending to.
cards.use_when: Reporting on email/SMS performance and deciding which segments to prioritize or suppress.
steps: Calculate revenue per recipient as total revenue divided by recipients, ideally per campaign and per segment.
Segment the list into buckets such as subscribers, repeat buyers (non-subscription), one-time buyers, and non-buyers, and compute RPR for each.

The source's subscriber segment returned roughly $8 RPR out of a 323,000-person list, while non-purchasers returned significantly less; treat the subscriber segment as the priority audience for reporting.
Go deeper by purchase behavior, e.g., six-pack vs 12-pack vs bundle buyers, to see which cohorts are most valuable.
Use this to suppress or deprioritize low-value groups, e.g., customers who only ever buy on discount; the source suggests suppressing them entirely rather than repeatedly paying to reach them.
Export customer-level purchase history and use AI or spreadsheet analysis to estimate long-term customer value over defined time windows.
caveats: RPR values are specific to the source's list and cohort definitions; the $8 figure is an example, not a benchmark.
Customer-level analysis requires exporting and joining order data, which the source calls more difficult than campaign-level RPR.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Map subscription churn peaks and intercept them
cards.summary: Understand the three churn peaks in a subscription (day one, ~day 28, and ~day 31–45) and deploy education and gifts to reduce them.
cards.use_when: Reducing subscription churn and building the post-purchase communications calendar.
steps: Expect a large day-one cancellation spike from customers who subscribed only for the discount; the source notes these customers were likely never going to stay, and this spike heavily skews overall churn numbers.
Counter it in the first seven days with communication: tell them what to expect, the feeling/effect, quality, product-use cases, and how to consume it, plus customer reviews.
Anticipate a second peak around day 28 when the billing reminder triggers, and a third in the roughly day 31–45 window; plan messages before each.
Use subscriber-only giveaways that cost little, e.g., entering anyone subscribed past the 27th into a draw for more of the product they already subscribe to.
Make it easy to cancel; the source notes forced minimum subscription terms are no longer legally viable and argues you should give people a fast off-ramp instead.
Track churn by period: the source moved from 24% churn in Q4 to 17% by focusing on this, with a stated goal of sub-5% aggregate churn.
caveats: The 24%→17% and sub-5% figures are the source's own numbers and goals; churn rates vary widely by category and price point.
Reducing churn is described as more product-dependent than tactic-dependent at their stage.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Pre-empt the four stated cancellation reasons with downgrades and alternatives
cards.summary: When subscribers cancel, they cite four reasons; build specific save paths for each instead of a generic discount.
cards.use_when: Designing cancellation flows and retention offers for subscription or repeat-purchase products.
steps: Recognize the four reasons the source hears on cancellation: can't afford it, have too much product, the effect isn't what they wanted, or found another brand.

For 'too much product,' offer education on alternate uses (e.g., mocktail recipes, giving it to a friend) and offer to downgrade: 12-pack to six-pack, or a smaller format with fewer milligrams or fewer cans.
Where users want control, offer a self-dosing format so they can make the product into whatever drink they want.
For 'too expensive,' treat price as the likely root cause and consider discounts or incentives rather than just product changes.
For 'effect isn't what I wanted,' focus on usage education and expectation-setting in earlier onboarding.
Build these as selectable paths in the cancellation flow so the reason routes to the right save action.
caveats: The four reasons are what customers told the source; your cancellation reasons may differ, so collect your own verbatim data first.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Send plain-text founder and team emails to build retention
cards.summary: Use plain-text, non-designed emails from the founder, support, and product team as a low-cost retention channel.
cards.use_when: Planning the monthly retention email calendar and deciding what non-promotional content to send.
steps: Send plain-text emails with no graphics from the founder, from customer support, and from product development on a roughly monthly cadence.
Use them for product education: step-by-step guidance on exactly how and when to use the product for maximum output, which the source says is under-taught.
Use them for non-revenue communication: the source cites an email teasing a launch and a livestream that generated about $40,000 with nothing purchasable except a footer link.
For smaller brands, lean into being the underdog and tell people you are a small business that appreciates their business; the source notes this works better before scale.
Time plain-text sends to relevant moments, such as price changes or tariff-related news, using playful, honest framing.
Segment by cohort so the copy speaks natively to the specific customer.
caveats: The $40,000 email result is a single example, not a promise.
Founder-voice messages lose effectiveness at scale, per the source.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Run response-driven campaigns to improve deliverability and engagement
cards.summary: Prompt customers to reply or submit content so list engagement and inbox placement improve while generating user content.
cards.use_when: Trying to lift email engagement or sender reputation, or needing user-generated content for retention and social.
steps: Diagnose the goal: the source ran a themed campaign because spam/deliverability was a problem and they needed mass replies, since replies are one of the few ways to prompt action.
Create a simple participation mechanic tied to a cultural moment.
Run it for a full month, collecting submissions and having the team rate/score them, then communicate back what people sent and what can be made with the product.
Feed the resulting user content back into emails and social.
Incentivize reflection on the product: invite customers to submit an image of the product or how they use it.
caveats: The source links the campaign to improved response rate but gives no numeric benchmark, and reply-based deliverability effects vary by list and provider.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Turn loyal customers into marketers with one-person asks
cards.summary: Convert high-value customers into advocates by making the ask small and achievable rather than viral.
cards.use_when: Building referral and word-of-mouth programs for repeat buyers.
steps: Identify your highest-value customer cohort and speak with them directly where feasible; the source used to personally call top customers weekly.
Ask each customer to tell exactly one person—not five—because a one-person ask is achievable and more likely to be done.
Personalize the request by calling out that the referred person is a friend of theirs so they are motivated to make it a good experience.
Leverage existing distribution: if you have a large social following, offer co-branded posts with influencers and creators, trading brand distribution for better rates and stronger partnerships.
Recognize that a referred customer avoids acquisition cost, which the source calls game-changing for unit economics.
caveats: The one-person ask and weekly calls are the source's practices, not tested benchmarks; do not assume a specific referral rate.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Fund a surprise-and-delight budget at the CX layer
cards.summary: Give customer service a discretionary budget to over-deliver on problems, because the perceived value of the product far outweighs its cost.
cards.use_when: Setting customer service policy and deciding how to handle damaged, missing, or unsatisfactory orders.
steps: Separate budgets: keep a discount budget and a separate surprise-and-delight ('wow') budget that the CX team can use at its discretion.
When an order arrives damaged or crushed, replace it generously (the source sends back a six-pack) and tell the customer to keep or give away the original.
For problems, over-deliver relative to the complaint; the source argues that net of true COGS, the extra goodwill revenue from a large order or word of mouth usually exceeds the give-away cost.
Treat the wow moment as a trigger for word of mouth, especially when the product is displayed in the customer's home or expresses their identity.
Attach a dedicated person to own this and respond across channels: the source hired a head of customer engagement to handle the wow budget and answer every comment and DM across seven channels daily.
caveats: The source's cost-justification is a judgment based on product COGS and perceived value; it may not hold for low-margin or low-visibility products.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Product selection: require repeat purchase, an emotional effect, and efficient packaging
cards.summary: Choose products that evoke a feeling or behavior change, support repeat purchase, and can ship in a small efficient parcel.
cards.use_when: Evaluating new product lines or SKUs for an ecommerce catalog.
steps: Prioritize products that facilitate a personal, repeatable experience: the source cites hydration/electrolyte packets and fragrance as categories where the customer buys again because they feel the effect.
Favor categories with repeat consumability so each purchase reopens the acquisition window.
Design the item to ship in a small parcel that fits a sleeve or can be fulfilled at volume; avoid large or bulky formats that inflate shipping cost and EBIDTA impact.

Bring in packaging/logistics expertise early to engineer the parcel size, as the source cites Native engaging a shipping specialist up front and describes cents-per-unit savings compounding into large annual figures.
Watch input costs (plastics, cardboard, aluminum) and tariffs, since material costs and packaging changes affect unit economics.
If a packaging change costs slightly more but reduces breakage, run the net math: the source changed cans because too many were crushing.
caveats: The $17-cent-per-unit and $8-million examples are the source's own figures from their operations, not a general benchmark.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Product expansion: compete on format and effect, not just flavor
cards.summary: Differentiate by matching products to effects and occasions instead of adding more of the same flavor variation.
cards.use_when: Planning a product-line expansion or deciding how to position new SKUs on shelf and online.
steps: Assess the shelf at retail: the source observes products are typically merchandised in threes (e.g., an original, a variant, and a flavor).
Choose a differentiation axis other than flavor count, such as effects (energetic vs relaxing) or dayparts (morning vs night, going out vs winding down).
Walk your own category's retail shelf and analyze how the products marry together and how many facings fit on the shelf; the source describes this exercise as very useful before expanding.
Match the product experience to the occasion the customer wants it for, rather than adding undifferentiated SKUs.
Bring in a formulator and a retail veteran to pressure-test the expansion roadmap and shelf realities.
caveats: The shelf-in-threes observation is a general pattern the source noticed, not a rule.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Build product feedback loops with post-purchase surveys and reviews
cards.summary: Capture first-time, repeat, and non-purchasers' input through post-purchase surveys, automated review requests, and follow-on outreach.
cards.use_when: Designing a process to feed customer data into product development, marketing, and sales outreach.
steps: Send a post-purchase survey asking how they heard about you, what they expect from the product, and where they expect to use it.

Treat the 'how did you hear about us' answer as a last-touch attribution signal, since customers reliably recall what they touched last even if multi-touch attribution is noisy; the source argues this should be treated as law and piped into Slack (an easy Zapier integration).
Trigger automated review requests when the product arrives, so positive reviews come in quickly.
Use a positive review plus a repeat-purchase signal to trigger a subscription offer at a better discount.
Flag unusually large orders (e.g., 48+ or 64 cases) so sales or community teams can follow up on what event or use case is driving the purchase.
Layer cohorts for feedback collection: first-time purchasers, repeat purchasers, and non-purchasers all have different experiences to mine.
caveats: Self-reported attribution is anecdotal and can be inaccurate; the source treats it as a directional signal alongside more rigorous measurement.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Weigh building in public against key-man risk and stop-start effects
cards.summary: Publishing company metrics and founder content can lower CAC and open doors, but stopping it can reverse gains and creates key-person dependency.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether the founder or brand should publicly share metrics, revenue, and process content as part of acquisition and brand strategy.
steps: Map your brand-building approach: some brands (cited: Represent, Minted New York, Cadence) share product development and story rather than granular financials, which the source calls comparatively safe.

If you share numbers, count the benefits: signaling to the market (investors, acquirers, competitors, potential employees), attracting retail partners, and trading distribution for better tech and partnership terms.

Account for the cost: the source reports disproportionate advantage while posting consistently, but a drop in CAC benefit if you stop, and describes stopping during COVID-era interruption as having an effect.

Recognize key-man risk: if the public face of the brand stops posting or changes their presented persona, the source argues the brand can suffer; make the public-building plan feasible long-term and build a real moat.
Broaden participation by having more of the team share the spotlight so the story does not depend on one person.
The source, having built this way, says if starting over they would not go as deep publicly, though they still see the reach as worth it.
caveats: The CAC-lowering and door-opening benefits are the source's own experience, not measured benchmarks.
This is presented as a double-edged sword; the source explicitly says they would dial it back if starting again.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a personal content system: pillars, weekly debrief, no AI voice
cards.summary: Run a structured weekly content process around a few pillars, with human-written copy and past-performance analysis.
cards.use_when: Planning a founder-led content or social calendar that supports an ecommerce brand's acquisition.
steps: Define a small number of content pillars: the source uses the brand, the agency/learnings (paid media, email, SMS, creative), and personal life and family.
Hold a weekly one-to-two-hour debrief to verbally brainstorm topics that are timely or personally important, then have writers turn those into drafts in your own voice.
Keep the copy human-written; the source's only AI use is analyzing which past posts performed organically, then reworking a strong performer into a new format (e.g., tweet to graphic).
Maintain a running Google Doc of current interests and projects that you update every couple of weeks as the topic source.
Use a project/projection/reflection rhythm: talk about what you are going to do that week, then report back on what happened and what you learned.

If budget is limited, use scheduling/writing tools and a trending-post discovery tool for inspiration, and study a low-cost solo-entrepreneur content course to understand paid/organic principles (verify current tool names and pricing, as they change).
caveats: The source credits a specific low-priced LinkedIn course and creator; no results are given for that course, and tooling pricing and features change over time.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Route acquisition and spend decisions through people with media-buying experience
cards.summary: Understanding how to deploy paid spend without emotional attachment to the money is a durable skill that can drive both brand building and agency work.
cards.use_when: Deciding who should own paid acquisition, or whether to build a brand versus run media buying as a service.
steps: Recognize that a strong media buyer is someone who can spend aggressively without being emotionally tied to each dollar; founders spending their own money often struggle with this.

If you are a product person without acquisition skill, you become dependent on others for growth decisions; the source argues you need enough paid-media literacy to know what a good marketer looks like.
Consider that agency and performance backgrounds make good founders or co-founders for brands, since they bring tested growth knowledge and spend discipline.

When evaluating a rollup or portfolio strategy, avoid a single centralized CMO across brands that target different customers; the source cites this as the core mistake of certain ecommerce rollup models.
If your product category has high barriers to entry (e.g., regulation or specialized marketing knowledge), expect fewer but larger competitors and plan accordingly.
The source's view is that whoever can spend the most wins at scale, so control of acquisition capability is a strategic asset.
caveats: The claim that 'he who can spend the most wins' is the source's opinion, not an established rule, and it ignores creative and product differentiation.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Reduce operating friction by non-negotiable morning routines
cards.summary: Deliberately delay caffeine and avoid email and breakfast early in the day to protect focus.
cards.use_when: Structuring a founder or operator workday around store and team demands.
steps: Delay caffeine rather than consuming it immediately on waking, as the source reports this works well for them.
Skip eating breakfast first thing if it helps focus; the source reports this has been working for them.
Avoid touching email in the morning; the source has an assistant lock their inbox and pre-filter what requires a reply, with everything else addressed around noon.
Apply the freed focus time to tasks with compounding value for the store, such as offer planning or content debriefs.
Treat these as personal experiments, not universal prescriptions; test each habit and keep what actually works for you.
caveats: These are the source's personal routines with no measured productivity results; skip or adapt based on health needs.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Evaluate 3PL and CX tooling for customer-experience dashboards, not just shipping
cards.summary: Prefer fulfillment partners with visibility into customer experience so service teams need fewer touchpoints to resolve issues.
cards.use_when: Choosing or renegotiating a 3PL or fulfillment partner.
steps: Rank 3PL candidates on whether they offer a customer-experience dashboard that gives clarity into individual customers and orders.
Prioritize partners that reduce the number of customer conversations your CS team must have, because handling deflection saves labor cost over time.
Treat the source's stated willingness to pay 10x for this capability as a signal of how valuable the visibility is, not as an actual pricing standard.
Use customer-level visibility to inform retention and follow-up actions like review requests and large-order outreach.
Check the current platform capabilities directly, since the source references a specific partner they were about to work with.
caveats: The 10x willingness-to-pay claim is the source's opinion, not a calibrated benchmark.
The named partner is described as one they were about to work with, so no results can be implied.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx
